Q192.L1t: Criminal liability for helping with a crime is analyzed under common law doctrines of accomplice liability, conspiracy, and the elements of burglary and larceny.
Q192.L2t: At common law, conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to commit an unlawful act, and accomplice liability requires that the helper intend to aid the crime.
Q192.L3t: The friend only pretended to join and intended from the start to have the young man arrested, so he never truly agreed with the young man and never shared any purpose of seeing the theft succeed.
Q192.L4t: The friend is not guilty of any offense, because he lacked the genuine agreement and the intent to further the theft that conspiracy and accomplice liability require.
Q192.L2f: At common law, conspiracy is complete only when a participant takes a substantial overt act toward the crime, and mere words of agreement are never enough.
Q192.L3f: Under the common law, a person who drives a burglar to the scene and waits outside is a principal in the second degree, and his private motive for helping is irrelevant to liability.
Q192.L4f: The friend is guilty of burglary, because he drove the young man to the house and thereby became a participant in the break-in.

Q193.L1t: The Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment limits how state and local governments may treat different groups of people.
Q193.L2t: In Plyler v. Doe, the Supreme Court considered a state law that denied public education to children who were illegal aliens.
Q193.L3t: The Court has held that illegal aliens are not a suspect class and education is not a fundamental right, yet it still struck down a bar on schooling their children because it imposes a lifelong penalty on children who are not responsible for their status and does not substantially further a substantial state interest.
Q193.L4t: The ordinance is invalid because excluding undocumented children from school over an unpaid fee is not substantially related to an important governmental interest.
Q193.L2f: In Plyler v. Doe, the Supreme Court held that illegal aliens are a suspect class, so any law treating them differently must satisfy strict scrutiny.
Q193.L3f: The constitutional test for this fee turns on whether the extra cost of hiring bilingual teachers places an excessive financial burden on the school system, and the Equal Protection Clause is concerned with that burden.
Q193.L4f: The ordinance is invalid because requiring the school board to hire additional bilingual teachers places an undue burden on the public school system.

Q194.L1t: Contracts for the sale of goods are governed by the Uniform Commercial Code, which sets rules for delivery, acceptance, and remedies.
Q194.L2t: A C.O.D. term means the buyer pays on delivery, and the buyer here accepted and paid for the 490 widgets that were tendered.
Q194.L3t: Under the perfect tender rule, a seller must deliver exactly the quantity promised, so delivering 490 of 500 widgets is a failure to perform the contract as written, and the buyer's acceptance of part does not waive its claim for the shortfall.
Q194.L4t: The buyer will recover because the manufacturer did not deliver all 500 widgets it promised and so failed to perform its contractual obligation.
Q194.L2f: A C.O.D. shipping term means the seller bears all risk and may not be held liable for any quantity shortfall once the buyer has inspected the goods.
Q194.L3f: A breach of contract supports recovery only if the missing performance is so substantial that it defeats the essential purpose of the agreement, and a shortfall of two percent does not.
Q194.L4f: The buyer will recover because the manufacturer's failure to deliver the remaining widgets was a material breach of the contract.
